  • How many calories do you need during pregnancy?
Pregnancy

How many calories do you need during pregnancy?

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy increases the need for nourishment, but “eating for two” does not mean doubling portions. Calories provide energy; they do not measure all the vitamins, minerals or protein you need. A useful plan considers your usual intake, health, pregnancy stage and growth rather than imposing one daily number or judging every bite.

There is no single calorie target for everyone

Energy needs depend on body size, age, activity, pre-pregnancy weight, pregnancy stage and whether you are carrying one baby or more. Illness, nausea, diabetes or other medical needs also affect the plan. A figure such as 2,000 calories is a general reference, not a prescription for every pregnant person.

Ask your maternity clinician or dietitian how to adapt your usual eating pattern. A calorie total alone cannot guarantee adequate nutrition or a healthy pregnancy, and feeling hungry does not mean you have failed to follow a rule. Your needs can change during pregnancy.

Trimester estimates differ between guidelines

For a singleton pregnancy starting at a healthy weight, CDC and ACOG describe usually no additional calories in the first trimester, about 340 extra daily in the second and about 450 extra daily in the third. These are estimates above usual needs, not the whole day’s intake or a compulsory allowance for everyone.

UK NHS advice uses a different general estimate: around 200 extra calories daily in the final three months. Do not add the UK and US numbers together or assume one estimate fits your body. Follow your local maternity team’s personalized advice, with attention to food quality, symptoms and growth.

In early pregnancy, regular nourishing meals may be more useful than trying to add a fixed amount. If nausea makes meals difficult, smaller frequent meals and tolerated foods may help. Persistent vomiting or poor intake needs treatment, not pressure to meet a number.

Twins and other multiple pregnancies

Multiple pregnancies often need more energy and a different weight-gain plan. ACOG’s general advice gives about 600 extra calories daily for twins, but this is not a universal third-trimester-only rule or a number to add again to the singleton increment. Discuss timing, portions and nutritional needs with the team.

Triplets or more, growth concerns, severe nausea and other complications need individualized specialist advice. Do not simply multiply a single-baby chart or delay support until the third trimester. Extra food should still provide varied nutrients rather than only more calories.

Starting pregnancy underweight or still growing

People who were underweight before pregnancy, adolescents who are still growing, or those with difficulty eating enough may need additional energy and nutritional support. The amount is individual; age or BMI alone does not determine a safe meal plan.

Tell the team about food insecurity, restrictive eating, previous eating disorders, significant weight loss or trouble gaining as expected. They can assess intake, symptoms, blood results and fetal growth and arrange dietitian support. More food may help, but persistent problems should not be managed by guessing alone.

A higher starting weight does not mean a weight-loss diet

If you began pregnancy overweight or with obesity, the recommended weight-gain range and energy plan may differ. That does not automatically mean you should cut calories, skip meals or try to lose weight. NICE advises against intentional weight loss during pregnancy because of possible harm to the baby.

Focus on adequate, varied food and suitable activity with your care team. Gestational diabetes or other conditions may require a specific eating and monitoring plan, not an unsupervised restrictive diet. Do not use slimming medicines or supplements as a pregnancy nutrition strategy; discuss all products with the prescriber.

Weight changes are a guide, not a weekly test

Weight gain includes the baby, placenta, fluids and changes in your own tissues. It is not all body fat or a direct measure of overeating. Early gain may be small or absent, while later gain is usually more gradual; the source’s fixed monthly or weekly figures are not rules for every pregnancy.

US recommendations use pre-pregnancy BMI and number of babies to estimate total gain. For example, CDC gives 25 to 35 pounds, about 11.5 to 16 kg, for a singleton pregnancy starting at a healthy BMI. Other starting BMI categories and twins have different ranges. These are discussion guides, not a diagnosis or a target to achieve by a particular week.

Monitoring approaches also differ: CDC encourages agreed tracking, while NICE does not recommend routine repeated weighing without a clinical reason. Decide with your team whether, how often and how to weigh, especially if numbers cause distress. Baby growth and clinical findings matter alongside any weight trend.

Choose foods that provide more than energy

Build variety from whole grains, beans and other pulses, protein foods, fruit and vegetables, calcium-rich dairy or suitable fortified alternatives, and appropriate amounts of unsaturated fats. Include leafy greens, yellow or orange vegetables and vitamin-C-containing fruit; use safe iron-rich foods and drink fluids regularly. Food safety remains important during pregnancy.

If you need more intake, practical additions might be yogurt or a fortified alternative with fruit, wholegrain toast with a protein food, or porridge made with milk. Portions and ingredients change the calorie content, so no pictured snack or combination is an exact prescribed amount. Choose foods you tolerate and can access.

If gain is greater than expected, review the whole situation with the team. They may suggest reducing frequent sugary drinks or foods high in added sugar and saturated fat while keeping nourishing meals. Not all processed foods are low in nutrients, and you do not need to eliminate every favourite food. Avoid assuming rapid change is simply overeating.

Supplements may still be needed even with adequate calories. Follow local advice on folic acid, vitamin D and any indicated iron or other nutrients; requirements and doses are individual. Do not double products or take high-dose supplements without advice, and avoid vitamin-A/retinol supplements in pregnancy.

When food or weight changes need medical help

Contact your maternity team promptly for persistent vomiting, inability to keep food or fluids down, weight loss, very dark or reduced urine, or dizziness and weakness. Inability to keep food or fluids down for 24 hours is a reason to seek help, but do not wait that long if you are dehydrated or unwell. Treatment can include pregnancy-suitable anti-sickness medicines and fluids.

Sudden swelling of the face or hands, severe persistent headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs or feeling very unwell needs immediate maternity assessment for possible pre-eclampsia. A rapid weight change is not a reason to assume you should restrict food. Seek emergency help for collapse, a seizure or severe breathing difficulty.

Do you need to count every calorie?

Most people do not need to count every bite. Some benefit from a dietitian-guided record for a specific medical or nutritional reason. Focus on regular meals, variety, comfortable portions and the agreed follow-up plan rather than daily perfection or frequent weighing.

If tracking triggers anxiety, guilt, restriction or an eating-disorder relapse, tell the team and ask for a different approach. A balanced eating pattern supports health but does not guarantee that everything is fine. Bring questions and new symptoms to antenatal care without blaming yourself for weight changes.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC and ACOG estimates are general US guidance; NHS uses a different UK additional-energy estimate, so advice should be individualized.

ACOG multiple-pregnancy advice and CDC weight ranges do not establish one rule for all multiples or all pregnancy stages.

NICE NG247, January 2025, advises against intentional pregnancy weight loss and routine repeat weighing without clinical reason.

Current NHS supplement and pre-eclampsia advice distinguishes nutritional support from warning symptoms needing medical assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record meal patterns, nausea, fluid intake, any weight tracking agreed with your team, and questions. Notes cannot calculate a safe personal calorie prescription, diagnose malnutrition, confirm fetal growth or rule out pregnancy complications.

When to seek help

Do not start a weight-loss diet, slimming product or high-dose supplement in pregnancy without appropriate medical review. Seek prompt help for persistent vomiting, poor fluid retention, reduced urine, weight loss or weakness. Severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling, pain below the ribs or marked illness needs immediate maternity assessment; collapse, seizure or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • You do not need to double portions, and 2,000 calories is not a universal pregnancy target.
  • US and UK trimester estimates differ; use them as context for a personal plan, not combined rules.
  • Twins, adolescence, starting weight and medical conditions can change needs.
  • Adequate nutrients matter as well as energy; intentional weight loss is not recommended during pregnancy.
  • Persistent vomiting, dehydration or sudden pre-eclampsia symptoms need assessment rather than calorie adjustments.

Frequently asked questions

How many extra calories are needed for twins?

ACOG gives a general estimate of about 600 extra daily for twins. Needs and timing vary, so seek an individual plan; do not add this again to a singleton increment or apply a third-trimester-only multiplication rule. Triplets or more require specialist advice.

Should I eat more if I was underweight?

You may need additional energy and nutrition support, particularly if still growing or struggling with intake. The amount depends on your circumstances. Discuss symptoms, food access, weight trend and baby growth with the team.

Should I eat less if I was overweight?

Do not automatically restrict calories or try to lose weight. An individual plan may use different energy or weight-gain goals while protecting nutrition. NICE advises against intentional pregnancy weight loss; ask for professional support.

Must I count calories?

Usually not. A record may be useful for a specific reason when agreed with a dietitian. If counting or weighing causes distress or restrictive eating, ask for another approach.

Why do US and UK numbers differ?

They are general guideline estimates, not direct measurements of your needs. CDC and ACOG describe about 340 extra in the second trimester and 450 in the third for a healthy-weight singleton pregnancy; NHS general advice describes about 200 extra in the final three months. Use local individualized advice, without adding them together.

Does slow weight gain mean the baby is not growing?

Not necessarily. Weight alone cannot determine fetal growth or nutrition. Report concerns so the team can assess intake, symptoms and growth; do not force a fixed weekly increase or ignore persistent poor intake.

Can I replace meals with supplements?

No. Supplements address particular needs and do not provide a complete substitute for meals. Follow the agreed pregnancy supplement plan without doubling doses or using retinol-containing products.

When should vomiting prompt help?

Seek prompt advice if vomiting persists, you cannot keep food or fluids down, lose weight, pass little or dark urine, or feel dizzy or weak. Do not wait 24 hours when dehydrated or very unwell. Severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling or pain below the ribs also needs immediate maternity assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
